question.text: A promoter of 'Narmada Developers' wants to raise INR 75 crore via structured private credit, using listed promoter shares as collateral, to avoid further equity dilution. Per Chapter 9, why is 'promoter financing' a legitimate private-credit use case for a Cat II debt AIF?

answer.text: Because SEBI mandates Cat II AIFs to fund promoters exclusively.
Because promoter financing is guaranteed by LIC.
Because Cat II AIFs receive RBI subsidies on promoter loans.

Because promoter financing lets founders retain a respectable stake (often targeted at ≥20% of paid-up capital) for management control and promoter status at IPO listing, while private credit fills a gap banks cannot.

explanation.text: The Logic: Chapter 9: 'Founders and promoters … have the challenge of retaining respectable stakes … usually desired at a level not below 20% of the paid-up capital of the company. Such stakes help them to retain management control and remain in the status of promoters when the company goes for listing. … In such cases, private credit can help promoters and start-up founders to shore up their stakes by promoter financing through structured debt.' Promoter shares can be used as collateral for such structured private credit. The Trap: Options A, B and C invent regulatory mandates or guarantees that do not exist for Cat II AIFs. Note: Use only the workbook rationale — the ≥20% paid-up capital target for retaining promoter status at listing and the use of promoter shares as collateral are both directly stated in Chapter 9.
